context: marine-works-led · piling & tidal/weather windows drive the programme

brief.intro: New to this project type? A jetty, quay or berth is a marine structure — piles driven into the seabed, a deck cast or set on top, and berthing furniture (fenders, bollards, dolphins) fixed to it so ships can safely tie up and load or unload. Unlike a building, most of the work happens over or in water, using a mobilised marine spread (barges, piling rigs, dredgers) that only operates in workable tide and weather windows. The structure itself is largely an enabler; the real planning risk is marine piling productivity, achieving design water depth by dredging, and — on fuel or product berths — the fire-fighting and utility piping systems that make the berth safe to load hazardous cargo.

scope.name: Marine investigation & mobilization
scope.desc: Geotechnical/metocean confirmation and mobilizing the marine plant spread (piling rig, jack-up barge, survey craft).

scope.name: Marine piling
scope.desc: Driving or drilling steel tubular or concrete piles for the berth, trestle and dolphins.

scope.name: Pile caps & deck structure
scope.desc: In-situ concrete pile caps and the deck slab or precast deck panels forming the working surface.

scope.name: Berthing & mooring furniture
scope.desc: Fenders, bollards, and mooring/breasting dolphins that absorb impact and hold the vessel.

scope.name: Dredging & scour protection
scope.desc: Achieving design water depth in the approach channel and berth pocket, and armouring the seabed against current scour.

scope.name: Approach trestle
scope.desc: The elevated causeway connecting an offshore berth back to shore, where the berth is not shore-attached.

scope.name: Electrical, lighting & cathodic protection
scope.desc: Berth power, navigation/deck lighting, and the system that stops submerged steel piles corroding.

scope.name: Fire-fighting & utility piping
scope.desc: Foam/deluge systems and bunkering or product-transfer piping — required on fuel and product berths.

scope.name: Instrumentation & berthing aids
scope.desc: Docking aids, mooring-load monitoring and SCADA tie-in to port control.

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & handover
scope.desc: Load-testing berth furniture and proving the berth with a live berthing trial before handover to the operator.

glossary.plain: the rubber or foam unit on the berth face that absorbs a ship's impact energy.
the deck-mounted fitting a ship's mooring lines are tied to.
a separate small marine structure, outside the main berth face, that a ship leans against or ties off to.
an electrical system (anodes or impressed current) that stops steel piles corroding in seawater.
the floating plant used to drive piles offshore, jacking itself clear of the water to work like a fixed platform.
rock or armour placed around piles and the seabed to stop currents washing the foundation away.
the limited hours of workable tide, wave height and wind speed in which marine plant can safely operate.
removing seabed material to reach the design water depth a vessel needs to berth safely.

must_get_right: Marine piling productivity and tidal/weather windows set the real pace — plan around workable days, not calendar days.
Marine plant (barges, piling rigs, dredgers) is a mobilised, shared resource — its mobilisation/demobilisation and weather standby time drives both cost and float.
On fuel or product berths, fire-fighting/foam and utility piping are safety-critical and gate berth acceptance — treat them as a distinct system, not generic MEP.
Dredging and scour protection are usually on the critical path to achieving design water depth ahead of the first berthing trial.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Marine activities are durationed against marine-plant productivity rates (piles per workable week), not generic civil productivity. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Marine works (piling, dredging, furniture set) run on a tide- and weather-dependent calendar with a modelled allowance for non-workable days by sea state and wind speed; landside works (electrical, MCC-type buildings if any) run a standard calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs marine mobilization → piling → pile caps & deck → berthing furniture set → cathodic protection & electrical energisation → berthing trial → handover, with dredging to design depth proceeding in parallel but converging before the trial. Piling productivity and weather/tidal downtime typically drive the critical path more than deck or electrical works.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Metocean and tide data validated at design; the marine plant spread is mobilised once for the duration of piling; seabed conditions match the geotechnical investigation; a disposal site for dredged material is available and permitted.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Marine plant (jack-up barge, piling rig, dredger) is a scarce, mobilised resource shared across the works; sea-state and weather windows constrain daily working hours; environmental/dredging permits and silt-curtain requirements gate dredging start; vessel traffic must be coordinated with the port authority throughout.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: weather/tidal downtime, marine plant breakdown or unavailability, geotechnical variation causing pile refusal or over-drive, and dredging permit delay. Schedule contingency is held around the piling and dredging fronts rather than spread thinly across the network.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the marine plant — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
